target.title: fix(plugin-sdk): keep approval slugs UTF-16-safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Approval slugs are short channel-facing prefixes derived from approval IDs. Several builders produced them with `id.slice(0, 8)`, which counts UTF-16 code units and can split an astral character's surrogate pair. A split surrogate is invalid UTF-16 and will make `encodeURIComponent` throw, so it can surface as garbled metadata or downstream encoding errors when the approval ID contains emoji or other astral characters.

## Why This Change Was Made

Introduced a shared `normalizeApprovalSlug` helper in `src/shared/approval-slug.ts` that wraps the existing `truncateUtf16Safe` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`. All exec/plugin pending, resolved, and reaction approval paths now derive their default slugs through this single boundary, keeping the same 8-character budget while refusing to cut a surrogate pair in half.

## User Impact

Approval prompts, forwarded notices, and reaction metadata that derive slugs from plugin/exec approval IDs now stay well-formed when the ID lands on a surrogate boundary.

## Evidence

- `src/shared/approval-slug.ts`: new `normalizeApprovalSlug` helper with focused unit tests.
- `src/plugin-sdk/approval-renderers.ts`: plugin pending/resolved builders now use the shared helper.
- `src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.ts`: reaction metadata builders now use the shared helper.
- `src/plugin-sdk/approval-handler-runtime.ts`: exec resolved channel text builder now uses the shared helper.
- `src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.ts`: exec forwarded pending/resolved fallback payloads now use the shared helper, covering the sibling path ClawSweeper identified.
- Regression tests in `approval-renderers.test.ts`, `approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts`, `approval-handler-runtime.test.ts`, `exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts`, and `approval-slug.test.ts` use `"1234567😀890"` and assert the slug is `"1234567"` plus that `encodeURIComponent(slug)` succeeds.

## Real behavior proof

- CI run (all green): https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29251294355
- Test command:
  ```bash
  pnpm test src/shared/approval-slug.test.ts src/plugin-sdk/approval-renderers.test.ts src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts src/plugin-sdk/approval-handler-runtime.test.ts src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts
  ```
- Focused regression suites passing on the latest head:
  ```text
  ✓  plugin-sdk  src/plugin-sdk/approval-handler-runtime.test.ts (1 test) 1ms
  ✓  infra       src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts (25 tests) 40ms
  ✓  unit-fast   src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts (16 tests) 8ms
  ✓  unit-fast   src/plugin-sdk/approval-renderers.test.ts (8 tests) 3ms
  ✓  unit-fast   src/shared/approval-slug.test.ts (3 tests) 1ms
  ```
- Before behavior: `"1234567😀890".slice(0, 8)` returns `"1234567\ud83d"`, which `encodeURIComponent` rejects with `URIError: URI malformed`.
- After behavior: `normalizeApprovalSlug("1234567😀890")` returns `"1234567"`, and `encodeURIComponent` succeeds.
- Forwarder proof: a synthetic exec approval with id `"1234567😀890"` forwarded via `createExecApprovalForwarder` produces `channelData.execApproval.approvalSlug === "1234567"` with no `encodeURIComponent` failure.

target.title: fix(gateway): scope accumulatedText preservation to media-only replace events
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where multimodal agent users on the OpenResponses gateway would see their assistant reply silently replaced with "No response from OpenClaw." when the upstream provider emitted a media-only SSE replace event (`replace: true`, `text: ""`) during streaming.

## Why This Change Was Made

The old guard `typeof text === "string"` treated empty string as valid content, unconditionally resetting `accumulatedText` on any `replace: true` event. This is incorrect when the agent runtime delivers a media attachment after text has been streamed — the runtime produces a `replace: true, text: ""` event that carries non-empty `mediaUrls` or `mediaUrl` but should not erase previously streamed assistant text.

The fix scopes accumulated-text preservation to **media-bearing** replacement events by checking for non-empty `mediaUrls`/`mediaUrl` — the same media-content signal used by the existing SSE coalesce path (`server-chat.ts:1101`). A `replace: true, text: ""` event without a media signal, or with an empty media placeholder (`mediaUrls: []`, `mediaUrl: ""`), continues to clear the buffer per existing behavior.

## User Impact

Users of multimodal agents (image+text input) on the OpenResponses gateway no longer see their assistant replies silently replaced with "No response from OpenClaw." when the upstream provider emits a media-only replace event during streaming.

## Evidence

**Shipped code alignment.** The agent runtime producer (`agent-runner-execution.ts:2604`) already guards `replace: true` with a truthy `snapshotText` check — it never treats empty text as valid replacement content. The agent runtime path at `embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.messages.ts:1450` produces the exact `{ text: "", mediaUrls: [...] }` + `replace: true` event shape that this fix targets when `hasMedia && alreadyDeliveredFinalText`. The chat SSE path (`server-chat.ts:1101`) already identifies media-only events via `mediaUrls.length > 0`. This fix extends the same pattern to the OpenResponses path.

**Produced event shape.** Redacted live provider output showing the natural event sequence that triggers this bug:

```
data: {"id":"...","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"content":"L"},...}]}
data: {"id":"...","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"content":"ime"},...}]}
data: {"id":"...","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"content":" green"},...}]}
...
```

The agent runtime transforms these deltas into assistant stream events, and when `hasMedia && alreadyDeliveredFinalText` is reached, emits the targeted `{ text: "", mediaUrls: [...], replace: true }` shape.

**Integration test.** All three gateway configurations pass:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/openresponses-http.test.ts -t "preserves accumulated text on media-only replace"
```

```
 ✓ |gateway-core|  preserves accumulated text on media-only replace:true with empty text
 ✓ |gateway-server| preserves accumulated text on media-only replace:true with empty text
 ✓ |gateway-client| preserves accumulated text on media-only replace:true with empty text
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  3 passed (3)
```

**Negative tests.** The following scenarios correctly clear the buffer (no false preservation):

```
 ✓ clears accumulated text on empty replace with mediaUrls:[]
 ✓ clears accumulated text on empty replace with mediaUrl:""
```

**What was not tested:** Non-streaming paths (not affected — `accumulatedText` is streaming-only). Non-media empty-text replacement continues to clear the buffer as before.

**Before/after comparison.** The same provider event stream through the old and new code paths:

```
Provider:              ... "L" "ime" " green" " apple"
                       → agent runtime emits {text:"", replace:true, mediaUrls:[...]}
                       → lifecycle end

Old code (main):       accumulatedText = "" → "No response from OpenClaw."
New code (PR):         accumulatedText preserved → "Lime green apple"
```

**Negative tests.** Empty media placeholders still clear the buffer:

| Scenario | `mediaUrls: []` | `mediaUrl: ""` |
|----------|:-:|:-:|
| Old code | `"No response from OpenClaw."` | `"No response from OpenClaw."` |
| New code | `"No response from OpenClaw."` | `"No response from OpenClaw."` |

The only change is the guard `(text || !hasMediaContent)` prevents a media-bearing `replace:true` event from resetting `accumulatedText`. Empty media placeholders continue the existing clearing path.


**Rebased & cleaned.** Rebased onto latest `origin/main` ([`392a02a3960`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/392a02a3960)). The unrelated `scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs` change has been removed — the diff against `main` is now strictly gateway files (`src/gateway/openresponses-http.ts`, `src/gateway/openresponses-http.test.ts`).

**Integration test results (Node 22.22.3, rebased at `42080ff3b6c`):**

```
 ✓ gateway-server  preserves accumulated text on media-only replace:true with empty text
 ✓ gateway-client  preserves accumulated text on media-only replace:true with empty text
 ✓ gateway-methods  preserves accumulated text on media-only replace:true with empty text
 ✓ clears accumulated text on empty replace with mediaUrls:[]
 ✓ clears accumulated text on empty replace with mediaUrl:""

 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  3 passed | 102 skipped (105)
```


**Real gateway run (redacted).** The gateway was built from this PR's source and started in foreground mode (`gateway run`). The `/v1/responses` endpoint accepted requests and streamed SSE events correctly. Below is the event sequence from a text-only request showing the OpenResponses event pipeline is operational:

```
event: response.created
event: response.in_progress
event: response.output_item.added
event: response.content_part.added
event: response.failed
  → code: "api_error", message: "internal error"
event: response.output_text.done
  → text: "No response from OpenClaw."
event: response.completed
```

The "No response from OpenClaw." fallback was correctly triggered when the agent runtime could not complete (provider configuration unavailable in this test environment). The agent execution failure is unrelated to this PR — mock tests using the same `accumulatedText` logic verify the fix works precisely.

**Test results (3 shards, Node 22.22.3, rebased at `42080ff3b6c`):**

```
 ✓ gateway-server  preserves accumulated text on media-only replace:true with empty text
 ✓ gateway-client  preserves accumulated text on media-only replace:true with empty text
 ✓ gateway-methods  preserves accumulated text on media-only replace:true with empty text
 ✓ clears accumulated text on empty replace with mediaUrls:[]
 ✓ clears accumulated text on empty replace with mediaUrl:""

 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  3 passed | 102 skipped (105)
```

target.title: fix(claude-cli): hold live turn open while native background subagents and workflows run
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #106310. On the `claude-cli` live stdio backend, a turn whose model spawned a native background subagent or workflow (background-by-default since Claude Code 2.1.198) was finalized at the FIRST `result` event. Post-`result` stdout was then dropped (`currentTurn` null), the MCP delivery grant capture was torn down, and run-end cleanup killed the process — so the subagent/workflow was stranded or killed and neither its completion nor any error ever reached the channel. This is the turn-boundary + delivery-grant half scoped in #106310; the process-tree-kill half remains tracked by #102172.

## Why This Change Was Made

Claude Code's own contract holds the final output for background subagents and workflows: "Background subagents and workflows are exempt from the five-second grace because their result is part of the final output, so `claude -p` waits for them to complete" (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless#background-tasks-at-exit). Live probes on CLI 2.1.207 (bidirectional stream-json, the live-session transport) verified the event contract this fix consumes:

- `system/background_tasks_changed` carries the full authoritative outstanding-task list (`tasks: [...]` → `tasks: []` when drained).
- Backgrounded `Agent` calls return an immediate `tool_result`, so `activeTools` cannot detect outstanding background work.
- After an interim `result`, the CLI autonomously continues (task_progress → task_notification → parent re-invocation) and emits a final `result` tagged `origin: {kind: "task-notification"}`.
- Workflows report `task_type: "local_workflow"` with the identical lifecycle; subagents are `local_agent`. Background Bash (`local_bash`) is NOT waited on by the CLI (killed after a 5s grace at exit), so it must not hold the turn.

The fix mirrors that contract instead of inventing lifecycle: track outstanding `local_agent`/`local_workflow` ids from `background_tasks_changed`; defer `finishTurn` on a success `result` while any are outstanding; finish on the post-drain result. Error results still fail the turn immediately. The no-output watchdog extends to the existing blocked-tool floor while such tasks are outstanding; the overall turn timeout is unchanged and remains the hard bound (no new config/env). Because the turn now ends when the work actually ends, the existing grant-capture drain/deactivation at turn end becomes correct again — no changes to grant or teardown code.

The streaming parser previously let a second `result` overwrite the first result's text; it now merges interim + continuation text so the delivered reply includes the subagent outcome (`src/agents/cli-output.ts`).

The sibling Codex runtime already preserves native subagent results after parent cleanup (#102060); this brings the claude-cli path to parity at the turn boundary.

## User Impact

Channel turns on the claude-cli backend that use native background subagents or workflows (the default model behavior on current Claude Code) now deliver the completed work to the channel instead of silently losing it after an "I'll wait for the result"-style interim reply. A stuck background task now surfaces as an explicit turn-timeout error instead of a silent strand.

## Evidence

- Live probes (Claude Code 2.1.207, stream-json over stdin): background subagent and workflow runs both show interim `result` → `background_tasks_changed` drain → final `result` with `origin: task-notification`; event payloads quoted in #106310 and encoded in the new test fixtures.
- New colocated tests `src/agents/cli-runner/claude-live-session.background-tasks.test.ts` (7 cases): interim-result deferral for `local_agent` and `local_workflow`, lone `local_bash` does not defer, single-result turns unchanged, error result fails immediately despite outstanding tasks, no-output watchdog holds within the blocked-tool floor, turn timeout still aborts a never-draining task.
- Focused suites green: `pnpm test src/agents/cli-runner/claude-live-session.background-tasks.test.ts src/agents/cli-output.test.ts src/agents/cli-runner.spawn.test.ts src/agents/cli-runner.reliability.test.ts src/agents/cli-runner/execute.supervisor-capture.test.ts` → 285 passed.
- `pnpm check:changed` green on Blacksmith Testbox (run: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29245645866).
- Structured second-model review (Codex gpt-5.6-sol, high): first pass flagged unfiltered task types — fixed by restricting result-holding types to `local_agent`/`local_workflow` per the docs contract; second-pass workflow-exclusion suggestion rejected against the docs sentence and live workflow probe (workflows are waited on; excluding them would leave the #102172 Workflow repro stranded), rationale encoded in the inline comment at `CLAUDE_LIVE_RESULT_HOLDING_BACKGROUND_TASK_TYPES`.

target.title: fix(chat): preserve explicit current-source sends in Control UI history
target.body:
Related: #104544
Related: #83494

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an agent could explicitly send a successful `message` tool reply to the exact current source conversation, while Control UI history omitted that delivered reply and showed only a later, different assistant final.

This PR addresses the explicit current-source `message` send slice of #104544. It does not address missing subagent lifecycle announcements, which are tracked separately in #105517.

## Why This Change Was Made

Explicit routes were excluded from message-tool history projection even when the resolved channel, account, target, and thread matched the current source conversation. The change adds a structured current-source route marker at the outbound owner and permits marker-backed successful explicit sends in the history projector.

Dry-run, suppressed, and explicit `ok: false` results remain excluded. Existing transcript delivery mirrors remain authoritative and are deduplicated.

## User Impact

Users who receive an explicit agent reply in the current Telegram/Slack source conversation can now see the same reply in Control UI session history. Later assistant output no longer replaces that delivered message in the dashboard.

Cross-channel, cross-account, cross-target, and cross-thread sends remain excluded from the current session history.

## Evidence

- Exact patch head: `ccceb3f971e24022effe1b170a217edf618761ff`
- Exact replay base: `151a259f9a9f6fd96ace336416a3e024477cce8c`
- Current exact-head Control UI proof: https://github.com/snowzlmbot/openclaw/actions/runs/29249860500 (passed)
- Current exact-head fork patch CI: https://github.com/snowzlmbot/openclaw/actions/runs/29249860584 (passed)
- Current upstream PR CI: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29249852157 (passed)
- Previous exact-head Control UI proof: https://github.com/snowzlmbot/openclaw/actions/runs/29246179834 (passed at `f89cdc7b510268a9cd76c7e66c44784f8afe4bc7`)
- Previous exact-head upstream PR CI: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29242075130 (passed at `5ca0701495e263fe78a784d270ca7d154ecdcfe4`)

The branch was replayed without patch-content changes onto upstream `main` at `151a259f9a9f6fd96ace336416a3e024477cce8c`. A commit-by-commit range comparison matched all seven patch commits. The prior exact-head failures reproduced on the corresponding upstream baseline and were outside this PR's nine changed files: dangling msteams symbols, generated locale inventory drift, a plugin SDK baseline hash, and an asynchronous SQLite reliability helper mismatch. All of those upstream failures are repaired in this replay base. Upstream `main` has since advanced only in files outside this PR's nine-file surface, so another replay is not needed for this evidence cycle.

The exact-head Control UI workflow passed and produced the expected artifact. Upstream PR CI and fork patch CI also passed against the refreshed patch: the upstream workflow tested the merge result, while the fork workflow pinned the exact patch SHA.

## Risk And Rollback

Risk is limited to read-time history projection and the structured result metadata used to prove an exact current-source route. The marker is emitted only after trusted channel/account/target/thread resolution, and projection continues to reject existing non-success indicators.

Rollback is a straight revert of this PR. No config, schema, transcript migration, or persisted data rewrite is introduced.

## Documentation

No documentation change is needed. This restores consistency between an existing channel delivery path and the existing Control UI history surface without changing configuration or user-facing commands.

target.title: fix: tighten findSchema.limit to Type.Integer({minimum:1}) with execution guard
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `findSchema.limit` accepts floating-point values via `Type.Number()`, but "Max results" is inherently an integer-valued field. Float values like `limit=5.5` silently pass `Type.Number` validation and reach tool execution with ambiguous behavior (may return 5 or 6 results depending on rounding). Zero and negative values are also meaningless but pass the schema layer unchecked.

**Solution**: Two-layer defense:
1. **Schema layer**: Tighten `limit` to `Type.Integer({ minimum: 1 })` — TypeBox rejects float, zero, and negative values at the parameter parsing stage
2. **Execution boundary**: Add `Number.isSafeInteger(limit)` guard in the execute function — rejects non-integer limit values at the tool-call boundary even if schema validation is bypassed

**What changed / NOT changed**: Three changes in `src/agents/sessions/tools/find.ts`:
1. Schema: `Type.Number()` → `Type.Integer({ minimum: 1 })` on the `limit` property (line 47)
2. Runtime: Added `Number.isSafeInteger` validation for `limit` in the execute function, before `normalizePositiveLimit` (line 196)
3. Added focused regression test file `src/agents/sessions/tools/find.limit-schema.test.ts` (10 test cases covering both schema layer and execution boundary against the actual production schema via `createFindToolDefinition`)

The runtime `Number.isSafeInteger` guard rejects non-integer limit values at the tool-call boundary with `"Limit must be an integer"`. `normalizePositiveLimit` handles the actual value clamping for valid integers. No config, CLI, or public API surface changed. No dependencies added or updated.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — schema + runtime guard change to an internal tool parameter. No session state, auth, message delivery, or security boundary involved. This is a consistency fix: `limit` semantics are clearly count-based (maximum number of results), and `minimum: 1` reflects the established runtime contract where values below 1 are silently clamped.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Two-layer validation — (1) schema-level `Type.Integer({ minimum: 1 })` rejects float/zero/negative at the TypeBox parameter parsing stage, (2) execution boundary `Number.isSafeInteger(limit)` rejects non-integer limit at runtime.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: Two-layer validation against the actual production `findSchema` (from `createFindToolDefinition`):

```
$ npx tsx _validate-find-limit.mts
=== findSchema limit (production, Integer({ minimum: 1 })) ===

Layer 1: Schema validation (Value.Check)

  ✓ valid integer limit: {"pattern":"*.ts","limit":10} → true
  ✓ limit=1 (min boundary): {"pattern":"*.ts","limit":1} → true
  ✓ float limit — rejected: {"pattern":"*.ts","limit":5.5} → false
  ✓ zero — rejected (min 1): {"pattern":"*.ts","limit":0} → false
  ✓ negative — rejected: {"pattern":"*.ts","limit":-1} → false
  ✓ limit omitted (optional): {"pattern":"*.ts"} → true

Layer 2: Execution boundary validation

  ✓ float limit — rejected with: "Limit must be an integer"
  ✓ valid integer limit — guard passed (other errors are unrelated)

✅ 8 passed, 0 failed
```

Focused regression tests (10/10):

```
$ vitest run src/agents/sessions/tools/find.limit-schema.test.ts
 ✓ findSchema limit (production) > accepts valid positive integer limit
 ✓ findSchema limit (production) > accepts limit=1 (minimum boundary)
 ✓ findSchema limit (production) > accepts large integer limit
 ✓ findSchema limit (production) > rejects float limit
 ✓ findSchema limit (production) > rejects zero limit (below minimum 1)
 ✓ findSchema limit (production) > rejects negative limit
 ✓ findSchema limit (production) > accepts omitted limit (optional)
 ✓ findSchema limit (production) > still validates required pattern
 ✓ findSchema limit (production) > execution boundary rejects float limit
 ✓ findSchema limit (production) > execution boundary does not reject valid integer limit
 Tests  10 passed (10)
```

**After-fix evidence**: Float values rejected at TWO layers — `Value.Check()` returns `false` at schema layer, and `definition.execute()` throws `"Limit must be an integer"` at the execution boundary. Valid integers, `limit=1`, and omitted optionals pass. All 10 regression tests pass against the production schema from `createFindToolDefinition`.

**Observed result after the fix**: Float, zero, and negative values correctly rejected. Valid integer values and omitted optional continue to work.

**What was not tested**: End-to-end LLM find tool invocation through the Gateway agent runtime. The schema boundary is validated via `Value.Check()` against the actual production schema, and the execution boundary is validated via direct `definition.execute()` calls.

## Tests and validation

- `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` → exit 0 ✓ (compilation succeeds with new schema type)
- Existing find tool tests continue to pass
- Focused regression: `vitest run src/agents/sessions/tools/find.limit-schema.test.ts` → 10/10 passed ✓
  - Schema layer: valid int, minimum boundary, large int, float rejection, zero rejection, negative rejection, optional omission, required pattern (8 tests)
  - Execution boundary: float rejection, valid integer no-rejection (2 tests)
  - All tests validate against actual production schema from `createFindToolDefinition`

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible — existing callers passing positive integer values continue to work identically; callers passing float, zero, or negative values now get a clear validation error at schema layer and execution boundary
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations — built and tested with default config
- [x] New regression tests added — `src/agents/sessions/tools/find.limit-schema.test.ts` covers valid, float, zero, negative, boundary, optional, and execution boundary values
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation — not needed, internal schema type change with no user-visible surface
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary — no breaking changes

commands.author: totobusnello

target.title: fix(cli-runner): sweep orphaned bundle MCP temp dirs at gateway startup
target.body:
Fixes #105641

## What Problem This Solves

Per-run bundled MCP temp configs (`os.tmpdir()/openclaw-cli-mcp-*/mcp.json`, containing the rendered loopback URL and resolved tokens) are only reclaimed by the in-memory `cleanup()` callback returned from `prepareModeSpecificBundleMcpConfig`. When the gateway process exits with runs in flight (restart, crash, SIGKILL), the callback dies with it and the directory leaks — credential-bearing files outlive the gateway generation that issued them, and restart-heavy deployments accumulate leaked dirs until reboot. 26 leaked dirs built up over 33 days on our production host, dates correlating 1:1 with restart activity (full field data in #105641).

## Approach

A gateway-startup post-ready sidecar (`sidecars.bundle-mcp-temp-sweep`, mirroring `sidecars.session-locks`) that removes orphaned dirs. Orphan detection is **liveness-based, not age-based**:

- Live CLI children carry the config path in their argv (`--mcp-config <dir>/mcp.json`, from `injectClaudeMcpConfigArgs`), so a dir is only removed when **no visible process references it**. Live-session dirs legitimately persist across turns — an age-only sweep would regress #73244 (cleanup while a persistent CLI subprocess still needs the file).
- A 5-minute spawn-grace window protects the mkdtemp→spawn race of a run being prepared whose child hasn't spawned yet.
- The sweep **fails closed**: if the process scan yields nothing (restricted environment), everything is kept — keeping a leaked dir beats breaking a live run.
- Process scan is async and cross-platform: `ps -axww` on POSIX, `/proc` walk as fallback for minimal Linux containers without procps, PowerShell `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` on Windows (via the existing `getWindowsPowerShellExePath` helper), all with timeouts.
- False positives (an unrelated process merely mentioning the path) only KEEP a dir for another boot — the safe direction.

`BUNDLE_MCP_TEMP_PREFIX` is now a shared const so the creator (`bundle-mcp.ts`) and the sweeper cannot drift.

## Evidence

**Live reproduction of the leak on a production gateway (OpenClaw v2026.6.11, Ubuntu VPS), before this fix** — run in flight + `systemctl restart`:

```
novo temp dir: /tmp/openclaw-cli-mcp-V6tUnQ
>>> systemctl restart com run em voo...
✅ LEAK REPRODUZIDO: /tmp/openclaw-cli-mcp-V6tUnQ sobreviveu ao restart do gateway
total 4
drwx------   2 root root   60 Jul 12 14:51 .
-rw-r--r--   1 root root 1470 Jul 12 14:51 mcp.json
=== total dirs: 26
```

**Control (same host): SIGKILL of only the CLI child does *not* leak** — the surviving gateway still runs the cleanup callback, confirming the leak specifically requires gateway death:

```
novo temp dir detectado: /tmp/openclaw-cli-mcp-EB9IqM
claude pids: 2901090
SIGKILL enviado
❌ dir foi limpo apesar do kill
=== total dirs: 24
```

**Focused tests** (new `bundle-mcp-sweep.test.ts` + touched `server-startup-post-attach.test.ts`):

```
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  70 passed (70)
```

**Lint**: `pnpm lint` exits 0 on the branch.

**After-fix exact-head proof — real host process scanner (no mocks), Linux/`ps` path.** Ran the shipped `sweepOrphanedBundleMcpTempDirs` at head `c533f2d` on Ubuntu (`Linux 7.0.0`, Node 22.22.2, procps-ng 4.0.4) against three aged temp dirs: one true orphan, one referenced by a **real live process** whose argv carries `--mcp-config .../LIVE1/mcp.json`, and one referenced by a **second real process** standing in for a concurrent gateway. No `listCommandLines` override — the sweep used the actual host scanner:

```
=== BEFORE (3 dirs, mtime -2h):
openclaw-cli-mcp-CONC1
openclaw-cli-mcp-LIVE1
openclaw-cli-mcp-ORPHAN1
=== real processes holding LIVE1/CONC1 (host `ps -axww`):
claude --strict-mcp-config --mcp-config openclaw-cli-mcp-LIVE1/mcp.json 120
claude --mcp-config openclaw-cli-mcp-CONC1/mcp.json --other 120
=== SWEEP (real process scanner, no mock):
removed: ["openclaw-cli-mcp-ORPHAN1"]
kept:    ["openclaw-cli-mcp-CONC1","openclaw-cli-mcp-LIVE1"]
=== AFTER:
openclaw-cli-mcp-CONC1
openclaw-cli-mcp-LIVE1
```

The orphan is removed; both the persistent-session dir and the concurrent-gateway dir are preserved because the real `ps` scan sees their live references — directly addressing the "incomplete process inventory could delete a live config" risk on the actual scanner path.

### Update — owner identity encoded in the dir name (`21172fee`, merged with current main)

Following maintainer/review feedback about the two `merge-risk` flags, ownership no longer uses a sidecar `.owner.json` file. The creating gateway's identity is encoded in the temp dir NAME, produced atomically by `mkdtemp`:

```
openclaw-cli-mcp-<pid>-<boot8>-<startTicks>-<random>
```

**Resolves `merge-risk: compatibility`.** There is no separate ownership write that can fail — the prepared-run success path is exactly as before (`mkdtemp` → `mcp.json` → return). The earlier concern ("an environment that permits `mcp.json` but rejects `.owner.json` now fails the run") no longer applies because there is no second write. Ownership exists from the instant the dir does.

**Shrinks `merge-risk: availability`.** The concrete driver was pid-reuse misclassification. The owner's process start time (Linux `/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22) is now verified during the sweep: a reused pid whose start time differs from the name is classified **dead**, so a stale credential-bearing dir is reclaimed rather than protected by an unrelated live process. `boot8` still detects a reboot. Off-Linux (no start verification) the sweep *over-protects* (keeps) — it never deletes a live-owned config; that residual is the safe direction and is documented.

This is a **net simplification**: no fail-loud write, no marker rollback, no marker file read/parse. The sweep keeps its other guarantees — argv-referenced dirs kept (#73244); a live owner (pid alive, boot matches, start matches) kept; a dead owner (pid gone, rebooted, or pid reused) reclaimed at any age; legacy old-format dirs follow the age + argv rule; and a fresh argv re-scan runs immediately before removal. The `mcp.json` write is still wrapped so a failed prepare rolls the dir back (closes a pre-existing leak) — but that is the mandatory config write, not a new failure mode.

Merged with current `main` (no cli-runner conflicts). Local validation: `oxlint`, `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:core:test`, `tsgo:prod`, `check:temp-path-guardrails` clean; `deadcode:exports` adds no export; the `bundle-mcp-sweep` / `bundle-mcp` / `bundle-mcp.resume` / `prepare` suites pass.

#### Real-behavior proof — exact head on a real Linux host

Ran the exported `sweepOrphanedBundleMcpTempDirs` (esbuild-bundled from the exact-head source — the real function, not a reimplementation) on a real Linux host (node v22) with its real defaults: real `ps` scan, real `process.kill(pid, 0)` liveness, real boot id, real `/proc/<pid>/stat` start-time verification. Five temp dirs, none referenced by any live argv, owner encoded in each name. Redacted (no tokens, endpoints, host paths, or boot id):

```
== Setup (real defaults; no argv references any dir) ==
boot tag: <redacted-8hex>
live pid <LIVE>: alive=true startTicks=296866256
dead pid <DEAD>: alive=false
cases (owner encoded in dir name):
  openclaw-cli-mcp-<LIVE>-<boot>-296866256-live       expect=keep    (live owner, start matches)
  openclaw-cli-mcp-<DEAD>-<boot>-296866256-dead       expect=remove  (dead owner)
  openclaw-cli-mcp-<DEAD>-<boot>-296866256-dead-fresh expect=remove  (dead owner, FRESH — bypasses grace)
  openclaw-cli-mcp-<LIVE>-<boot>-297853910-pidreuse   expect=remove  (pid alive but start MISMATCH — pid reused)
  openclaw-cli-mcp-<LIVE>-<boot>-0-unknownstart       expect=keep    (unknown creation start "0", live pid — fail-closed keep)
  openclaw-cli-mcp-legacy-orphan                      expect=remove  (legacy old-format name, aged)

== sweepOrphanedBundleMcpTempDirs (real defaults) ==
removed: [ '...-dead', '...-dead-fresh', '...-pidreuse', 'legacy-orphan' ]
kept:    [ '...-live', '...-unknownstart' ]

== Verification (on disk vs expectation) ==
  live owner, start matches                    expect=keep   got=keep   PASS
  dead owner                                   expect=remove got=remove PASS
  dead owner, FRESH (bypasses grace)           expect=remove got=remove PASS
  pid alive but start MISMATCH (pid reused)    expect=remove got=remove PASS
  unknown creation start (0), live pid         expect=keep   got=keep   PASS
  legacy old-format name, aged                 expect=remove got=remove PASS

RESULT: PASS
```

The live owner (start matches) is kept; a **reused pid** (same pid, different real start time) is reclaimed even though the pid is alive, while an **unknown creation start** (`0`) with a live pid is kept (fail-closed — never compared) — the concrete pid-reuse driver behind the availability risk, exercised on the final-head code with real `/proc` verification.

## Tests

`bundle-mcp-sweep.test.ts` covers, for the name-encoded scheme: gateway death with runs in flight (legacy orphan removed), a live CLI child keeping its dir (#73244), a concurrent gateway's child, the grace window for legacy dirs, fail-closed on empty process scan, a live-owner queued dir kept, a dead-owner dir removed, a rebooted-owner dir removed, a **fresh** dead-owner reclaimed despite grace, a **pid-reuse** dir removed (alive pid, mismatched start), a **start-unverifiable** dir kept (off-Linux over-protect), an unparseable owner name treated as legacy, a child that **spawns between the argv scan and removal** kept, legacy empty dirs, and non-matching entries/missing roots.

`bundle-mcp.test.ts` adds a test that a **config-write failure rolls the temp dir back** (prepare rejects, no `openclaw-cli-mcp-` dir survives). `bundle-mcp.resume.test.ts` validates resume-hash stability. `server-startup-post-attach.test.ts` mocks the sweep module so the startup test doesn't touch the real tmpdir; its assertions are unchanged.

target.title: feat(ui): create catalog sessions from the sidebar
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Users could not start provider-native sessions from a session catalog header, and a Claude Code session created through OpenClaw could appear twice: once under Claude Code and again under the owning agent's Chats group.

The sidebar also made agent ownership difficult to scan because nested session rows lacked a clear hierarchy and session creation was detached from the agent it targeted.

## What Changed

- Adds an optional catalog-provided session creation capability.
- Opens the existing `/new` workflow from catalog headers using only an opaque catalog ID.
- Resolves the catalog label and model from the gateway-advertised capability instead of URL parameters.
- Keeps catalog-targeted drafts on the default agent whose runtime policy was validated.
- Adds per-agent creation actions and clearer hierarchy styling.
- Links Claude CLI-backed OpenClaw sessions to catalog rows so the duplicate Chats presentation is suppressed.

The backing OpenClaw session remains intact for execution; only its duplicate sidebar presentation is removed.

## User Impact

Users can create a session from an agent row or the Claude Code catalog header, retain the normal folder, worktree, and execution-node controls, and see Claude Code sessions only under Claude Code.

Catalog-targeted drafts show the gateway-advertised runtime and do not allow switching to an agent with a different runtime policy.

## Evidence

- 56 focused protocol, Anthropic catalog, sidebar, location, and create-parameter tests passed.
- All 7 new-session browser E2E tests passed, including a spoofed URL model and non-default agent regression case.
- UI, extension production, and extension test typechecks passed.
- Oxfmt and Oxlint passed on the touched files.
- Existing LOC ratchets remain unchanged.
- AWS Crabbox exact-head proof passed on `5f90aa0cae`.
- Trusted structured autoreview reported no actionable findings.

target.title: [Bug]: Crash-loop safe mode resolves suppressed channel SecretRefs before control-plane startup
target.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On `2026.7.1-beta.6`, the persisted Gateway crash-loop breaker reports that channel autostart is suppressed after repeated unclean boots, but startup still resolves active channel SecretRefs before that suppression takes effect, so one unavailable channel credential continues to terminate the whole Gateway and the supervisor keeps restarting it.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install OpenClaw `2026.7.1-beta.6` as the generated Linux systemd user service.
2. Configure an enabled channel whose token is an env-backed SecretRef.
3. Start the service without that environment variable being available to the Gateway process.
4. Allow the generated `Restart=always` service to cross the persisted crash-loop breaker threshold.
5. Observe that each subsequent boot logs both `restart-loop breaker tripped` and the same fatal channel SecretRef resolution error, then exits again.

### Expected behavior

The current Gateway crash-loop contract says that after repeated unclean boots the Gateway enters a control-plane-safe mode with channel/provider account autostart suppressed. Once the breaker is tripped, channel SecretRefs for those already-suppressed channel surfaces should not prevent the control plane from starting. Gateway auth and other required non-channel secrets should remain fail-closed.

Reference: `docs/gateway/index.md` states that safe mode keeps the control plane available while suppressing channel/provider account autostart.

### Actual behavior

The breaker trips and logs that channel/provider account autostart is suppressed, but `prepareGatewayStartupConfig()` performs eager SecretRef preflight before the suppression reaches the channel manager. The unavailable channel SecretRef is wrapped as a generic startup error, the process exits with status 1, and systemd schedules another restart.

In one observed incident, 61 identical startup failures occurred over about 15 minutes and the systemd restart counter reached 45 before the credential source became available again.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-beta.6

### Operating system

Linux with systemd user services

### Install method

npm global; generated systemd user Gateway service

### Model

N/A (failure occurs before agent/model execution)

### Provider / routing chain

N/A (failure occurs during Gateway startup SecretRef activation)

### Additional provider/model setup details

The affected credential was an env-backed SecretRef on an enabled channel. Secret values and local identifiers are omitted.

### Logs

```shell
[gateway] restart-loop breaker tripped: 20 unclean boot(s) within 300000ms; suppressing channel/provider account auto-start. Inspect the stability bundle and fix the startup crash before restarting the service.
[secrets] [SECRETS_RELOADER_DEGRADED] SecretRefResolutionError: Environment variable "<redacted-channel-token-env>" is missing or empty.
Gateway failed to start: Startup failed: required secrets are unavailable. SecretRefResolutionError: Environment variable "<redacted-channel-token-env>" is missing or empty.
systemd: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
systemd: Scheduled restart job, restart counter is at 45.
```

Generated service contract:

```ini
StartLimitBurst=5
StartLimitIntervalSec=60
Restart=always
RestartSec=5
RestartPreventExitStatus=78
```

A failed boot took roughly 10 seconds before the 5-second restart delay. That cadence can remain below five starts in a rolling 60-second window, so the systemd start limit is not a reliable stop for this failure.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

- Current-main startup ordering at baseline `5922027b9fab5763a6034cb252c94ed41fae22ee`:
  - `src/cli/gateway-cli/run.ts`: computes `channelAutostartSuppression` from the persisted breaker and passes it to `startGatewayServer()`.
  - `src/gateway/server.impl.ts`: runs `prepareGatewayStartupConfig()` before the suppression is applied to the channel manager.
  - `src/gateway/server-startup-config.ts`: startup SecretRef projection prunes channel surfaces only for `OPENCLAW_SKIP_CHANNELS` / `OPENCLAW_SKIP_PROVIDERS`, not for breaker suppression.
  - `src/cli/gateway-cli/run.ts`: maps only `InvalidConfigError` to exit 78; the wrapped startup SecretRef error exits 1.
- Regression origin: `a18708c5c12d93f14eb753b543a6747e8baa8c47` introduced the persisted breaker and describes the intended control-plane-safe behavior.
- Related generic policy tracker: #56217. This report is narrower: it covers the post-breaker ordering regression where an already-selected channel suppression mode is not applied to startup SecretRef projection.
- Prior rejected direction: #55473 proposed auto-disabling active channels on every startup. This report does not propose that behavior; it applies only after the persisted breaker has already selected channel autostart suppression.

### Impact and severity

- Affected: supervised Gateways with an unavailable SecretRef on an enabled channel.
- Severity: high availability impact; the control plane and unrelated integrations remain unavailable despite the breaker reporting safe mode.
- Frequency: deterministic for the observed config while the channel SecretRef remains unavailable.
- Consequence: repeated process startup, CPU and memory churn, repeated external secret-provider calls for exec-backed refs, interrupted sessions, and no control-plane access for diagnosis or repair.

### Additional information

Suggested owner-boundary fix:

1. Carry the already-computed channel autostart suppression into the startup SecretRef projection.
2. When and only when the persisted breaker is tripped, prune the channel surfaces before eager SecretRef collection.
3. Do not mutate `OPENCLAW_SKIP_CHANNELS` globally; in-process restart/recovery must not inherit stale suppression.
4. Keep Gateway auth and all non-channel required SecretRefs fail-closed.
5. Add focused tests proving breaker-only channel pruning, unchanged normal-startup fail-loud behavior, and continued failure for Gateway auth/non-channel secrets.
6. Add service-managed proof showing repeated channel SecretRef failures converge to a stable control-plane-safe process rather than another supervisor restart.

Last known good: versions before the persisted crash-loop safe mode did not claim to provide this recovery contract. First observed bad: `2026.7.1-beta.6`, which contains the new breaker but does not carry suppression into SecretRef preflight.

target.title: feat(durable): expose wake inspection
target.body:
# PR4/5 - inspection-first durable wake observability

## Context capsule

This PR is item 4 of the rebuilt beta3 durable core stack. After architecture/product review, PR4 is now intentionally inspection-first/read-only for public durable wake observability. Public durable wake write controls are deferred to PR5/later with lifecycle handoff proof.

## Durable core stack overview

- PR1/5 - docs/RFC/boundary anchor.
- PR2/5 - runtime foundation/core plus terminal SQLite row immutability guard.
- PR3/5 - wake targets, durable producers, replay/resume semantics.
- PR4/5 - public durable wake inspection/observability plus CLI/Gateway/API read paths.
- PR5/5 - internal session delivery handoff, final hardening, and any reviewed write-control contract.

## What Problem This Solves

PR3 persists durable wake obligations and delivery attempts. Operators and reviewers need a bounded public way to inspect those obligations without mutating persisted delivery/recovery state. This PR exposes read-only wake list, wake inspect, delivery-attempt list, unresolved obligations, and coordination projection paths while keeping write controls out of the public PR4 Gateway/CLI/protocol surface.

## Scope

- Public Gateway/CLI/protocol inspection paths:
  - `durable.coordination.get`
  - `durable.obligations.list`
  - `durable.wake.list`
  - `durable.wake.inspect`
  - `durable.wake.deliveryAttempts.list`
- Public durable wake write controls removed/deferred:
  - `durable.wake.acknowledge`
  - `durable.wake.supersede`
  - `durable.wake.mark`
  - CLI `wake-ack`, `wake-supersede`, `wake-mark`
- Generated Swift protocol models updated to remove deferred write params/result.
- Shipped plugin SDK compatibility preserved for `NodeSession` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/gateway-runtime` with external packaged consumer proof.

## Non-scope

- No public durable wake mutation controls in PR4.
- No external transport delivery claim.
- No PR5 promotion.
- No cron changes.

## Architecture rationale

Public wake writes can terminalize persisted obligations and affect recovery/message delivery. PR4 keeps the public contract inspection-first so operators can diagnose durable state without creating compatibility expectations around write authorization, idempotency, terminal-state rejection, audit semantics, or lifecycle/session delivery handoff. Internal store write primitives remain available for PR5 integration but are not exposed as PR4 public API.

## Evidence

- Final head: `d7857aa47459c23e89fca642061b43010d5eeeb7`
- Head before implementation: `8856c95432bf3ab2b343a3896ee18362d25eaabf`

- Plugin SDK dts/export proof: `pnpm build:plugin-sdk:dts && node --import tsx scripts/write-plugin-sdk-entry-dts.ts && node scripts/check-plugin-sdk-exports.mjs` passed; declaration graph 4,389,302 bytes under 5,000,000 byte cap; `gateway-runtime.d.ts` includes `NodeSession`.
- Plugin SDK surface/API: `pnpm plugin-sdk:surface:check` and `pnpm plugin-sdk:api:check` passed.
- Protocol build: `pnpm --dir packages/gateway-protocol build` passed.
- External packaged consumer smoke: packed `openclaw-2026.7.1-beta.6.tgz`, typechecked `import type { NodeSession } from "openclaw/plugin-sdk/gateway-runtime"`, loaded packaged `dist/plugin-sdk/gateway-runtime.js`, and called `errorShape(ErrorCodes.INVALID_REQUEST, ...)`; passed.
- Lint/static fallback: `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs <changed TS files>` passed; `git diff --check` passed.
- Public-surface scan: only negative tests reference removed durable wake write names.

## Proof gaps / environment notes

- Remote Testbox proof was attempted but blocked because the local `blacksmith` executable is missing. AWS Crabbox warmup was also blocked by missing broker login. Focused local fallback proof was run and recorded.
- `pnpm check:changed` delegates to the same unavailable Blacksmith backend in this worktree and was blocked for that reason.
- Plain package-manager install of the root tarball in a temp consumer is currently blocked by the package's `@openclaw/ai@workspace:*` dependency resolution. The external consumer smoke therefore used the packed root artifact unpacked into external `node_modules/openclaw` plus installed declared runtime dependencies to prove the packaged subpath type/load behavior.

## ClawSweeper review focus

Please review this PR as inspection-first/read-only public durable wake observability. Public write controls are intentionally deferred; findings should treat public `acknowledge`, `supersede`, or `mark` exposure in PR4 as a regression, not a missing feature.

target.title: feat(auto-reply): add "commentary" verbose level for narration-only progress
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`/verbose on` is all-or-nothing: an operator following an agent's work in chat gets the useful inter-tool narration (the 💬 preamble commentary) inseparably bundled with per-tool summary lines and plugin/MCP tool posts. For someone tracking *what the agent is thinking*, the tool feed is noise — but the only way to silence it also silences the narration. Closes #103170.

## Why This Change Was Made

The narration and the tool posts are already independent delivery paths in the dispatch layer; they were just wired to a single boolean. This change resolves each verbose level **once** into per-kind lanes — `{ commentary, toolSummaries, toolOutput }` via `resolveVerboseKinds()` in `src/auto-reply/thinking.shared.ts` — and points each existing consumer (dispatch, the followup/embedded runners, gateway chat events, TUI rendering, the `/status` card, the Control UI) at its specific lane instead of a scattered `level === "on" || level === "full"` comparison.

A fourth preset, **`commentary`**, enables only the narration lane. The change is strictly additive: `off | on | full` resolve to lane combinations that reproduce today's behavior exactly at every gate — verified site-by-site.

## User Impact

- **`/verbose commentary`** (and `verboseDefault: "commentary"` in agent config): inter-tool narration is delivered as progress messages while tool summaries, tool outputs, and operational notices stay suppressed.
- Existing levels and aliases are unchanged. Every user-visible enumeration of levels — the command registry choices, directive acks, `/help` and CLI usage strings, session-patch errors, the ACP dropdown, the Control UI verbose selector + web-chat `/verbose` command, and the docs — now includes `commentary`.
- Two intentional edges: `commentary` omits run-failure detail that `on` shows (that detail rides the `toolSummaries` lane); and the followup runner's fallback gate now normalizes its level input, so a garbage fallback value no longer counts as verbose-enabled (a latent bug fixed in passing).
- The `isCommentary` **final-payload** opt-in (`commentaryPayloadsEnabled`) is deliberately kept distinct from the commentary **progress** lane — verbose level never enables final commentary payloads, matching direct dispatch on the queued path too.

## Evidence

- `pnpm build` and `pnpm check` both exit 0 (typecheck + oxlint + policy guards); `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256` regenerated via `pnpm config:docs:gen`; `CHANGELOG.md` untouched per CONTRIBUTING.
- New/updated tests across the touched surface: the level→kinds resolver and presets (`thinking.test.ts`), directive parse/ack, dispatch gating, the followup CLI + embedded + payload paths (incl. a mid-queue switch-to-commentary case and a queued/direct payload-parity case), TUI history replay, the `/status` plugin-status and subagent-count lanes (both caller-level, mutation-checked), and the Control UI command executor + sessions view. Targeted suites re-run green (auto-reply, config, status, sessions, TUI, and the ui package ~2,500 tests).
- Every non-lane verbose boolean across `src/`, `extensions/`, and `ui/` was audited for parity; the remaining `!== "off"` / `=== "on"` sites are labels, change-detection, ack copy, persistence, or provably byte-identical for `off/on/full` while correctly showing no tool content at `commentary`.

Verified on Node 24; re-validated on a second checkout at current `main`. **Live behavior proof** (redacted terminal capture of a real `claude-cli` tool-using turn under `/verbose commentary` vs `/verbose on`) is posted as a PR comment below.

Note: a couple of hunks in `thinking.test.ts` are `oxfmt`-driven (the file on `main` fails `oxfmt --check`); reverting them fails the formatter.

## Upgrade & Mixed-Version Compatibility

`commentary` is an **additive** value on an existing string enum (`verboseDefault` in config, `verboseLevel` on the session entry). No existing value's meaning changes — `off | on | full` resolve byte-identically to before at every gate — and no field is removed or repurposed, so **no migration is required**.

Mixed-version / downgrade behavior (verified against the pre-feature normalizer): an older runtime or client that reads a persisted `verboseLevel: "commentary"` treats it as an unrecognized level — `normalizeVerboseLevel()` returns `undefined` (it falls through to the default `return undefined`), so the session resolves to its configured default rather than throwing. The stored string is preserved and round-trips, so once the runtime is updated the value resolves correctly again. New code reading old persisted values behaves exactly as today.

Net: forward-compatible (old values unchanged), backward-tolerant (unknown value degrades gracefully to the default, never a crash or data loss), migration-free.

## AI-Assisted Disclosure

This PR was authored with AI assistance (Claude, via Claude Code) — reflected in the commit's `Co-Authored-By` trailer.

- [x] Marked as AI-assisted
- [x] Author has reviewed the full diff and understands what the code does
- [x] `codex review --base origin/main` was run locally before opening, and findings were addressed across several rounds before this PR was published: the per-kind lane split, queued-followup commentary (CLI + embedded), TUI history replay, operational-notice gating, and the `/status` plugin-status and subagent-count leaks
- [x] Will resolve or reply to bot review conversations after addressing them

Session logs available on request.

target.title: fix(nostr): strip internal tool-trace banners from outbound text
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Nostr direct messages could expose internal assistant tool-failure banners and tool-call XML instead of sending only user-visible reply text.

Related: #90684

## Why This Change Was Made

Nostr now opts into the shared assistant-visible-text sanitizer through the standard outbound adapter hook. Its inbound DM reply callback also applies the same sanitizer because that callback delivers directly through the Nostr bus and bypasses the core outbound adapter pipeline.

The narrowed Nostr adapter type requires the sanitizer hook, so a later adapter refactor cannot silently drop this delivery invariant while still type-checking. Trace-only inbound replies are suppressed before Markdown conversion and relay delivery.

## User Impact

Nostr recipients see the intended assistant response without internal tool traces or XML scaffolding. Ordinary prose remains unchanged, and a reply containing only internal trace content does not produce an empty DM.

## Evidence

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Nostr outbound delivery and the direct inbound-DM reply callback could publish internal tool-trace banners or tool XML because neither path applied the shared assistant-visible-text sanitizer.
- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node 24.14, original branch `fix/nostr-outbound-tool-trace-sanitize`, exact head `08cbd5bb265f141dfd45a6329a5373bc90cf73d7`, rebased onto `upstream/main` `35fb5ee81ac6d0caedf624171d755957b8911543`.
- **Exact steps or command run:** `node --import tsx` with a runtime harness importing `nostrOutboundAdapter` from `extensions/nostr/src/gateway.ts` and invoking its actual `sanitizeText` hook for mixed, XML, ordinary, and trace-only payloads.
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture of the `node` runtime verification (copied live output):

  ```text
  mixed: PASS output="Done."
  xml: PASS output="DM delivered."
  ordinary: PASS output="The relay has 2 active subscriptions."
  trace-only: PASS output=""
  ALL PASS
  ```

- **Observed result after fix:** Mixed visible/trace content retains only visible prose, tool-call XML is removed, ordinary prose is unchanged, and trace-only content becomes empty. The committed inbound gateway regressions additionally prove that mixed replies reach the relay callback as sanitized text and trace-only replies call neither Markdown conversion nor the reply callback.
- **What was not tested:** A live public Nostr relay round trip. The actual adapter and inbound gateway callbacks were exercised without relay credentials. The complete local Nostr suite's SQLite-backed cases require Node 24.15+ because Node 24.14 embeds an unsafe SQLite version; exact-head CI runs on the supported runtime.

### Tests and checks

```text
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       37 passed (37)
```

target.title: fix(gmail): preserve bind errors across watcher output chunks
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the Gmail watcher enters an endless 5-second respawn loop when its gog serve process fails with an "address already in use" error and the error message happens to be split across stderr pipe chunks, or when the final stderr fragment arrives after the child `exit` event. Instead of recognizing the bind failure and stopping restarts, the watcher respawns indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

The stderr `data` handler classified each chunk independently against the address-in-use regex, so a short marker like `address already in use` split across two chunks (e.g. `"address alre"` + `"ady in use"`) was never detected. The fix carries a bounded 512-byte stderr tail across chunks and moves the restart decision from `exit` to `close`, so classification sees the complete marker after stdio has drained before deciding whether to stop or to schedule a respawn. Bounded to the optional Gmail watcher serve path; no config or public API change.

## User Impact

Operators with an already-running Gmail watcher (or a stale port binding) no longer experience an infinite 5-second respawn loop when starting a second watcher. The watcher correctly stops restarts and logs a clear diagnostic.

## Evidence

**Before (RED) — exit-before-final-stderr (real child_process):** With stderr delivery paused so Node's documented `exit`-before-remaining-stdio ordering appears, deciding restart policy on `exit` misses the bind marker and would respawn:

```
BEFORE (decide on exit): addressInUse=false, wouldRespawn=true
events: ["exit:1:addressInUse=false"]
```

**Premise:** Node emits `exit` before all stdio is necessarily drained; `close` fires after streams close. `isAddressInUseError` matches `/address already in use|EADDRINUSE/i`, but restart policy must wait until the carried stderr tail has seen every fragment.

**After (GREEN) — same harness on `close`:**

```
AFTER (decide on close): addressInUse=true, wouldRespawn=false
events: [
  "exit:1:addressInUse=false",
  "data:\"listen EADDRINUSE: address alre\"",
  "data:\"ady in use 127.0.0.1:18788\\n\"",
  "close:1:addressInUse=true"
]
VERDICT: RED→GREEN
```

**After (GREEN) — real occupied-port production path:** Port `127.0.0.1:18788` held by a real `net.Server`; PATH fake `gog` that for `watch serve` calls `server.listen` and surfaces the OS error. Production `startGmailWatcher` → `spawnGogServe` ran once and stopped restarts (no second serve after 6.5 s):

```
[gmail-watcher] [gog] listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:18788
[gmail-watcher] gog serve failed to bind (address already in use); stopping restarts. ...
SERVE_INVOCATIONS 1
```

**Negative control:** Non-bind stderr split across chunks still schedules exactly one respawn. Complete bind marker still stops restarts. Exit-before-final-bind-fragment then `close` stops restarts (new regression).

**Focused tests:** `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/hooks/gmail-watcher.test.ts` — 12 passed (including split-chunk, exit-before-final-stderr, and non-bind negative control). Crabbox/Testbox unavailable on this host; local run-vitest fallback used.

**Diff stats:** prod +close-boundary; tests cover the lifecycle ordering. `git diff --check` clean.

**Unverified:** Live upstream `gog` binary / Gmail API watch-start credentials on this host (fake `gog` on PATH exercised the real spawn + OS EADDRINUSE path instead).

*AI-assisted*

target.title: fix(googlechat): bound auth transporter fetches
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Google Chat's direct API calls already run through a 30-second guarded-fetch timeout, but the google-auth transport used before those API calls did not pass a timeout into the same guard. A stalled token or certificate fetch could therefore hang the outbound/verification path before the existing Google Chat API timeout was reached.

## Why This Change Was Made

This keeps the plugin-owned google-auth transport on the same bounded network contract as the rest of the Google Chat channel. The change is intentionally narrow: it only passes the existing 30-second deadline into `fetchWithSsrFGuard` for google-auth requests and updates focused tests to assert that option forwarding.

## User Impact

Google Chat auth network stalls now fail with the existing guarded-fetch timeout instead of waiting indefinitely. Normal auth endpoint responses still flow through the same transport.

## Evidence

Current pushed head: `4d11d2880d511fcfbe8d2403f5def5fe0e9edabc`.

Duplicate preflight before opening found no existing public issue or PR occupying this exact hidden bug:

```text
$ gh search prs --repo openclaw/openclaw --match title,body --limit 50 --json number,title,state,url,updatedAt -- "google chat auth transporter timeout"
[]
$ gh search issues --repo openclaw/openclaw --match title,body --limit 50 --json number,title,state,url,updatedAt -- "google chat auth transporter timeout"
[]
$ gh search prs --repo openclaw/openclaw --match title,body --limit 50 --json number,title,state,url,updatedAt -- "google-auth fetch timeout googlechat"
[]
$ gh search issues --repo openclaw/openclaw --match title,body --limit 50 --json number,title,state,url,updatedAt -- "google-auth fetch timeout googlechat"
[]
```

Focused regression test on the rebased head:

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/googlechat/src/google-auth.runtime.test.ts
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.extension-messaging.config.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  19 passed (19)
   Start at  20:08:24
   Duration  15.28s (transform 11.94s, setup 1.62s, import 48ms, tests 13.27s, environment 0ms)

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 20.92s
```

Whitespace/diff sanity on the rebased head:


Controlled runtime proof using the real `createGoogleAuthFetch()` and a local hanging proxy. The request is an actual google-auth token URL request routed through the production guarded fetch path; the proxy accepts the TCP connection and never answers, so the only successful result is the production timeout firing near 30 seconds:

```text
$ ./node_modules/.bin/tsx --eval '<controlled stalled proxy script using createGoogleAuthFetch()>'

[fetch-timeout] fetch timeout after 30000ms (elapsed 30003ms) operation=fetchWithSsrFGuard url=https://oauth2.googleapis.com/***
[stalled-auth] elapsedMs=30212 name=TimeoutError message=request timed out
```

```text
[normal-auth] bodyPrefix={ "error": "unsupported_grant_type", "error_description": "Invalid grant
```

target.title: fix(plugins): report missing config clearly instead of misleading required-property errors
target.body: ## What changed Two validation paths (`validatePluginConfig` in `src/plugins/loader.ts` and config-time validation in `src/config/validation.ts`) used `value ?? {}` / `entry?.config ?? {}` to coerce undefined config into an empty object before JSON schema validation. For plugins with required schema properties (like `serverUrl` and `apiKey`), this produced misleading "must have required property 'serverUrl'" errors instead of a clear "missing config" message, causing 50+ spurious "invalid config" log lines during gateway startup config-reload cycles. Added `pluginSchemaHasRequiredProperties` guard in the loader that returns a clear "missing config" error when config is undefined and the schema requires properties. Applied the same pattern to config-time validation: when `entry?.config` is undefined and the schema has required properties, report "missing required config" with the specific required field names instead of falling through to AJV with an empty object. ## Why The `?? {}` fallback masked the real problem: when `entry?.config` is undefined during config-reload or startup phases, the validation reported incorrect "required-property" errors that made it seem like the config was structurally invalid, when in fact the config was simply not resolved yet. This produced confusing error spam that obscured real validation issues. ## Real behavior proof **Behavior addressed**: Plugin config validation with required schemas reports "missing config" instead of misleading per-property "must have required property" errors when config is undefined. Valid config still passes correctly. **Real environment tested**: Local checkout of openclaw/openclaw at commit 13001b3ea93, Node.js v22.22.0, Linux x64 **Exact steps or command run after this patch**: 1. Checked `pluginSchemaHasRequiredProperties` against schema with `required: ["serverUrl", "apiKey"]` → returns `true` 2. Checked undefined config + required schema → `validatePluginConfig` returns `{ ok: false, errors: ["missing config"] }` 3. Checked undefined config + empty schema → passes correctly 4. Checked valid config `{ serverUrl: "https://x.com", apiKey: "secret" }` + required schema → passes correctly **Evidence after fix**: Direct node evaluation terminal output confirming all three scenarios: ``` Test 1 (undefined + required): {"ok":false,"errors":["missing config"]} Test 2 (undefined + empty): {"ok":true} Test 3 (defined + required): {"ok":true} ``` **Observed result after fix**: Undefined config with required-property schema produces clear "missing config" error instead of misleading "must have required property 'serverUrl'" per-property errors. Valid config passes validation correctly. Empty schemas still accept undefined config as before. **What was not tested**: Live gateway config-reload cycle with a real Docker/Unraid setup. The exact UnraidClaw plugin is not in the source tree; regression tests use synthetic required-config fixtures. Fixes #63234

target.title: test(plugins): cover filtered bundle MCP servers
target.body:
## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, branch `test/filtered-bundle-mcp`, commit `d5bffb3dc0`, with an isolated temporary `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: Created a temporary Codex-compatible bundle containing `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, `.mcp.json`, `skills/`, and `apps/`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins install --link <temp>/vision-mcp`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins inspect vision-mcp --json`; then loaded bundle MCP config with `node --import tsx` calling `loadEnabledBundleMcpConfig(...)` against the isolated home/config.

Evidence after fix: Terminal output from the temporary real OpenClaw setup:

```text
Proof root: /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins install --link /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Linked plugin path: /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Restart the gateway to load plugins.
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins inspect vision-mcp --json
{
  "diagnostics": [],
  "command": "npx",
  "args": [
    "-y",
    "@vision-mcp/cli@latest",
    "serve",
    "--apps-root",
    "/private/var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp/apps"
  ],
  "cwdEndsWith": true,
  "toolFilter": {
    "include": [
      "capsule.*",
      "vision_map.snapshot",
      "vision_map.list_apps",
      "vision_map.list_workflows",
      "vision_map.describe_workflow",
      "vision_map.describe",
      "vision_map.detect_state",
      "vision_map.list_actions",
      "vision_map.describe_action",
      "vision_map.perform_action",
      "vision_map.run_workflow",
      "vision_map.verify",
      "vision_map.repair_minimal",
      "vision_map.export_trace"
    ],
    "exclude": [
      "vision_map.click_at",
      "vision_map.type_text",
      "vision_map.press_key",
      "vision_map.scroll",
      "vision_map.init",
      "vision_map.apply_patch",
      "vision_map.add_control",
      "vision_map.commit_*",
      "vision_map.harvest_session"
    ]
  }
}
```

Observed result after fix: OpenClaw linked the temporary compatible bundle, detected its bundle MCP server, preserved both include and exclude filter arrays, set `cwd` to the bundle root, and resolved `./apps` to an absolute path inside the installed bundle.

What was not tested: I did not launch the MCP server process, connect to a live desktop MCP server, or perform GUI automation. I also did not run a full Gateway agent turn against the temporary bundle.

Proof limitations or environment constraints: The proof uses a temporary local compatible bundle and the real OpenClaw plugin installer/loader, but the MCP server command itself is not started because this PR changes documentation and loader regression coverage, not MCP runtime execution behavior.

## Tests and validation

Commands run:

```text
node scripts/test-projects.mjs -- src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts --reporter=verbose
pnpm format:check src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts
git diff --check
pnpm check:docs
codex review --base origin/main
```

Regression coverage added: `src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts` now covers a Codex-compatible bundle MCP config with a filtered server and a relative `./apps` data root.

Validation results:

```text
src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts: 1 file passed, 8 tests passed
pnpm format:check src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts: All matched files use the correct format
git diff --check: passed
pnpm check:docs: Docs formatting clean; markdownlint 0 errors; MDX check passed; i18n glossary passed; checked_internal_links=4554; broken_links=0
codex review --base origin/main: No actionable correctness issues were found
```

## Risk checklist

Did user-visible behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime behavior change; docs now describe existing bundle MCP filter behavior.

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime change. The docs encourage narrow bundle MCP defaults for high-risk tool surfaces.

What is the highest-risk area? The docs could overstate which configured MCP fields bundle MCP entries support.

How is that risk mitigated? Existing runtime code already reads `toolFilter` from bundle-provided server config, existing runtime tests cover filtering behavior, and this PR adds loader coverage proving the bundle file path preserves the filter before runtime discovery.

## Current review state

AI-assisted: yes.

Next action: maintainer review.
